title: Why Recess Time-Out Doesn’t Work
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes the familiar sight of students dragging their feet toward an unsupervised or loosely supervised recess time-out, and questions whether this common consequence actually changes behavior. He argues that recess time-out is frequently ineffective for two related reasons: missing recess is often not a strong enough deterrent for many students, and repeated use with the same students causes them to internalize a 'this is who we are, we're the bad ones' identity rather than change their behavior. His proposed fix is simple but demanding: teachers should personally supervise recess time-out themselves rather than delegating it to another adult or leaving students unsupervised, even though this is inconvenient and costs the teacher a break. He explains that direct supervision communicates that the teacher genuinely cares, and that students should not be spoken to at all during the time-out, treating it as a serious, silent consequence. He closes with an anecdote about students from other classes expressing envious admiration that his students' teacher accompanies them to time-out, arguing that this personal investment, more than the time-out itself, is what changes behavior.
points: Recess time-out often fails to change behavior because missing recess is not a strong enough deterrent for many students.
Repeated use of the same consequence with the same students causes them to internalize a negative identity ('we're the bad ones') rather than improve their behavior.
The recommended fix is for teachers to personally supervise recess time-out themselves, rather than delegating it to another adult or leaving it unsupervised.
Teachers should remain silent during recess time-out, treating it as a serious, no-lecture, no-conversation consequence.
Personal supervision, despite being inconvenient for the teacher, communicates genuine care and is what ultimately makes the consequence effective.
quotes: They shuffle slowly toward a lunch table or an empty bench carrying a fluttering sheet of paper or a book with no bookmark. They often get a drink of water or use the restroom along the way, killing as much time as they can get away with.
Many, if not most, teachers use recess time-out as a consequence for poor behavior or missed homework, but does it really work?

Sadly, when you take a close look at who is on recess time-out week in and week out, it’s usually the same students. They look around and think, “Yep, this is my crew. This is who we are. We’re the bad ones.
By staying with them during recess, you are communicating to your students that they’re a priority for you and that you care about them and their behavior.
You want to impress upon your students that time-out is such an important consequence-sacred even-that no one is allowed to speak, not even the teacher.
Many times I’ve heard students from other classrooms say to my students. “You’re so lucky. Your teacher goes with you to time-out.
